sources.title: Search results on the Open Sicilian with 2...Nc6, Richter-Rauzer, Sozin, Four Knights (snippets only)
sources.publisher: Wholesale Chess, Wikipedia, Chessiverse via web search

overview: After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black has developed the knight to c6 before choosing a set-up, so the root is a crossroads: Classical (5.Nc3 d6), Sveshnikov (5...e5 after ...Nf6), Four Knights (5...e6), Kalashnikov or Lowenthal (4...e5), Accelerated Dragon (4...g6) and Taimanov-type lines (s1, s2, s3). White gets a development lead and kingside space, Black gets the open c-file and a central pawn majority, so the play is unbalanced and complex (s1). The Richter-Rauzer (6.Bg5) and Sozin (6.Bc4) lead to a race where White attacks on the kingside, often castling queenside, and Black counters with ...a6, ...b5 and c-file pressure (s2). Statistics are balanced (White 47.7%, Black 47.3% in 5.6 million Lichess games, per the Chessiverse page for the Four Knights) (s3).

white_ideas.idea: Richter-Rauzer 6.Bg5: pin Nf6, threaten to double Black's pawns with Bxf6, castle long and pressure d6 with a kingside pawn storm (f4, g4)
Sozin 6.Bc4: aggressive bishop on c4 hitting e6 and f7, castle kingside or queenside (Velimirovic Attack)
Use the lead in development and kingside space after 3.d4
Four Knights: Bg5 pins and prepares queenside castling and kingside pressure

black_ideas.idea: Pressure on the open c-file and use the central pawn majority
Timely exchange on d4 or ...e5 to reduce White's attacking control; Boleslavsky 6.Be2 e5 for independent play
Sveshnikov ...e5 gaining central counterplay and accepting the d5 hole

typical_structures.structure: Open Sicilian: White d-pawn exchanged for Black's c-pawn, White with e4, Black with d6/e-pawn centre and half-open c-file
Richter-Rauzer: d6 pawn as a long-term target; doubled f-pawns after Bxf6 gxf6 giving Black the bishop pair
Sveshnikov: Black pawns on d6/e5, with White's knight on d5 as an outpost (own understanding, unsourced)

character.notes: The open Sicilian is described as open and extremely complex with an opposite-wing race (s1, s2). The Richter-Rauzer is White's sharpest reply and gets very sharp if Black drifts (s4). The Classical lines are theory-heavy and pattern-based (s2). The Four Knights is more balanced but a 'theoretician opening' (s3). Overall Sharp is the best fit for the main lines, though some branches (Four Knights, Boleslavsky) are quieter.

gambit.notes: No material is given in the main lines; the c-pawn is exchanged for the d-pawn.

soundness.notes: Fully sound; 5.6 million Lichess games show near-equal scores (s3). Classical, Sveshnikov and Accelerated Dragon are all top-level choices.

structure.notes: Typical middlegame has the d-pawn traded, Black's half-open c-file and White's e4 pawn. The centre is partly open (s1). The Sveshnikov and Boleslavsky lines have Black ...e5 with a d5 hole and are more closed. Semi-open fits the Najdorf and Dragon anchors.

approach.notes: A crossroads of mainstream defences played by top players. Not a system. Standard.

level.notes: Chessworld says moderately theoretical, with accessible ideas for club players seeking active repertoires (s2). Chessiverse: a 'theoretician opening' where adherence to theory rises to 78% at 2500 (s3). The Sozin/Velimirovic and Richter-Rauzer lines have a lot of forcing theory (s1, s2). Black studies it. Advanced on memory, though the Four Knights and Boleslavsky are easier.

description.claim: 3.d4 immediately creates a dynamic and unbalanced struggle
description.note: Open and extremely complex per Wikipedia.

description.claim: White gains a central space advantage
description.note: White gets a lead in development and extra kingside space; the central pawn majority belongs to Black.

description.claim: Black obtains a semi-open c-file and a central pawn majority
description.note: Both are listed as Black's compensation.

description.claim: Promising rich, tactical counterplay for players who thrive on sharp, complex positions
description.note: True of the Richter-Rauzer and Sozin; less so of the Four Knights.

common_plans.claim: White: use space to launch a kingside attack (f4-f5 or g4-g5)
common_plans.note: Richter-Rauzer: f4, g4 and h-pawn advances.

common_plans.claim: White: control the d5-square and restrain Black's queenside activity
common_plans.note: d5 is more a hole White can't control in the Sveshnikov; no source frames White's plans this way.

common_plans.claim: Black: exert pressure on the c-file and generate queenside counterplay with the a- and b-pawns
Black: prepare the ...d5 pawn break to challenge the centre
common_plans.note: ...d5 is an equalising break in Scheveningen/Taimanov-like set-ups. In the Classical, Richter-Rauzer and Sveshnikov sources, Black's central ideas are ...e5 and exchanges on d4, not ...d5.
